ladder.analysis:
This story sits at the intersection of an unpopular six-month-old U.S.-Iran war and an intraparty Republican clash over how that war has been conducted. Massie is using impeachment as a mechanism to force a public reckoning over the legality and cost of military action, alleging Hegseth waged the war for more than 90 days without congressional authorization. The administration has defended Hegseth's conduct, and Republican leaders are expected to have the votes to block the impeachment attempt, with the House required to act by Thursday, just before lawmakers leave for an extended recess.

The backdrop is a costly and expanding regional conflict: independent Pentagon and CBO estimates put the price tag at over $33 billion and rising, while fighting has spilled into Saudi Arabia and Yemen through Iran-backed Houthi attacks, and Iran has publicly rejected U.S. overtures toward talks. Public opinion polling shows broad American opposition to the war, giving Massie's effort political salience even though it is unlikely to succeed procedurally.

stories.headline: Saudi Arabia warns of 'red line' after Houthi drone near Mecca; conflict escalates
stories.byline: International & World desk · anchored on Reuters, AP
body: Saudi Arabia said it shot down a Houthi drone south of the Islamic holy city of Mecca on Tuesday evening, prompting warnings from the Saudi-led coalition and the 57-nation Organisation of Islamic Cooperation, which called attacks on Mecca and Medina province an 'unacceptable and intolerable transgression.' The Houthis denied targeting Mecca, with military spokesman Yahya Sarea accusing Saudi Arabia of 'fabrications and lies' and stating that Houthi operations target 'oil facilities and military bases, and are far removed from the holy places.' Sarea also said the Houthis had launched drones and missiles in retaliation for more than 450 Saudi air strikes over the past week, and claimed they shot down a Saudi fighter jet over Marib province.

The incident came as the Houthis seized control of large swaths of Yemen's Red Sea coast, including the strategic port city of Mokha and Perim Island in the Bab al-Mandab Strait, the southern gateway to a key shipping route linking Asia and Europe via the Red Sea and Suez Canal. The Houthis said they pose no threat to international shipping but would target vessels from Saudi Arabia, which has relied on the Red Sea for oil exports since the Strait of Hormuz was effectively closed due to the US and Israel's war with Iran. Meanwhile, Saudi Arabia's key East-West Pipeline, used to transfer crude oil from the Gulf to the Red Sea port of Yanbu, was closed after being damaged in a strike the kingdom blamed on Iran-backed militias in Iraq. US Energy Secretary Chris Wright predicted oil would flow within days, though some experts said repairs could take more than a month.

Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman has personally pressed US President Donald Trump to take military action against the Houthis, but Trump has so far declined, offering only intelligence and targeting support, according to sources familiar with the matter. A senior Trump administration official said, 'We are in continuous dialogue with Saudi Arabia and the Republic of Yemen government regarding regional stability.' The United Nations Security Council held an emergency meeting where Yemen's government and Saudi Arabia called for more decisive action against the Houthis, who they accused of choking the Bab al-Mandab Strait to apply economic pressure. Council members agreed that freedom of navigation in the Red Sea must be maintained.

The escalation has deepened Yemen's humanitarian crisis. The International Organization for Migration reported that more than 90,000 people have been displaced by recent fighting, with director general Amy Pope warning that 'families are being forced to flee for the second or third time in this conflict, with almost nothing left.' The World Health Organization said at least 500 people had been killed since the start of August, including 297 in the previous week. Yemen's civil war, which began in 2014 when the Houthis ousted the government from Sanaa, has left more than 150,000 dead and triggered one of the world's worst humanitarian crises, with over 22 million people in need of aid, according to the UN.

The conflict is also putting pressure on Egypt, which depends on Suez Canal revenues. Houthi attacks in late 2023 had already reduced canal earnings by around $6 billion in 2024, according to the IMF, though revenues had recently recovered, rising 23% to $4.67 billion in fiscal 2025–2026. Stephan Roll of the German Institute for International and Security Affairs noted that the Houthis 'could actually interrupt, or at least significantly disturb, the connection between Asia and Europe.' Egypt has limited military options; its participation in the Saudi-led coalition is largely symbolic, and it has rejected a reported Houthi offer to discuss shipping security for fear of legitimizing the group. Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman traveled to Cairo on Tuesday seeking Egypt's support, but analysts say Egypt is likely to wait and see as it balances its alliance with Saudi Arabia against its own economic vulnerabilities.

stories.headline: Gaza building collapse kills 21, dozens missing under rubble
body: At least 21 people, including eight children, have been killed and dozens are missing after a war-damaged six-storey building collapsed overnight in the Tal al-Hawa area of Gaza City, local rescuers and medics said. The building, which had been left tilting dangerously after an Israeli strike more than a year ago, housed displaced families who had nowhere else to go, witnesses told the BBC. The Hamas-run Civil Defence agency said about 100 people were still under the rubble, and UN officials estimated between 70 and 100 were trapped.

Rescue efforts are proceeding slowly due to a severe lack of equipment. Civil Defence workers initially used their bare hands to dig, and UN agencies and an Egyptian team have joined the search. “We are still hearing voices from under the rubble, so there is still hope to find people,” said Raed al-Dahshan, director of the Civil Defence in Gaza City. Alessandro Mrakic, head of the UNDP Gaza office, said at the scene: “The situation, as you see, is tragic because we don't have the equipment and machinery that is needed. There are actually people digging with their bare hands.” He added that approximately 400 other war-damaged buildings across Gaza are at imminent risk of collapse, particularly as winter approaches.

Witnesses described the sudden collapse. “It felt like an earthquake. There was a loud sound and I couldn't stand up. Stones rained down on us and when I looked outside I saw a lot of dust,” Umm Mohammed Bakrun, a woman living in a nearby tent, told the BBC. Mansour Abu Mohammed said the building collapsed “in a few seconds,” adding: “Every day, a stone or a few stones would fall from it, but the people inside couldn't find anywhere else to live. I used to live next door to it and you could see that it was tilting to one side.” Locals said some 10 families had been living in the building's apartments.

The UN's humanitarian relief co-ordinator, Ramiz Alakbarov, said he was “devastated” by the reports and urged Israeli authorities to approve deliveries of heavy machinery for rescue operations, as well as tents and tarpaulins ahead of winter rains. Israel says its restrictions are meant to keep equipment out of the hands of Palestinian armed groups. The war, triggered by the Hamas-led attack on southern Israel on 7 October 2023, has destroyed or damaged an estimated 80% of all structures in Gaza, according to the UN. More than 1.9 million people — about 90% of the population — have been displaced, with 1.2 million living in tents or makeshift shelters. The Gaza health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the UN, reports more than 73,790 people killed since the war began.

stories.headline: Two sailors missing after tanker attacked in Strait of Hormuz; oil prices rise
body: Two sailors are missing and 23 others have been rescued following an attack on an oil tanker in the Strait of Hormuz, Oman's Maritime Security Centre said. The Panama-flagged El Gaia was being towed to an Omani port after a fire broke out in its engine room, with the vessel targeted 1.3 nautical miles (2.4km) north of the Musandam peninsula.

Conflicting accounts of the attack have emerged. Iran's Revolutionary Guards said Monday that the tanker hit naval mines and caught fire while passing through what they described as a restricted and unsafe route. The US military insisted the Iranian report was false, saying the tanker was struck by an Iranian missile last month and again by a drone over the weekend. The UK Maritime Trade Operations centre said it had received a report of a fire breaking out on board a vessel struck by an unknown projectile while transiting the Strait of Hormuz in the early hours of Sunday.

The attack follows a similar incident earlier this month that killed two Filipino sailors on the Saudi-owned oil supertanker Sidr. The Revolutionary Guards said that vessel caught fire after hitting a naval mine, but Saudi authorities said it was targeted by Iran, and maritime security firms reported it was hit by projectiles north of Musandam. The International Maritime Organization says at least 22 seafarers have been killed in 79 confirmed incidents in the Strait of Hormuz and the rest of the Middle East since the start of the US and Israel's war with Iran at the end of February.

In a related development, Iran's semi-official Fars news agency, linked to the Revolutionary Guards, reported that "enemy drones" had targeted two fishing boats in the strait overnight near the Iranian port of Kargan, about 80km (50 miles) north-east of Musandam. The agency cited the deputy governor of Hormozgan province as saying several fishermen were reported missing and a search-and-rescue operation was under way. Later, Capt Tim Hawkins, a spokesman for the US military's Central Command (Centcom), told the news website Axios that its forces had destroyed two boats which tried to steal a sea drone. "Iranian small boats recently attempted to take possession of a US unmanned surface vessel, but they were unsuccessful after Centcom forcefully responded," he said.

The Strait of Hormuz, through which a fifth of global oil and gas shipments usually pass, has effectively been closed due to Iranian missile and drone attacks on commercial vessels and a US naval blockade of Iranian ports. The US and Iran reached a preliminary agreement to end the war and reopen the strait in June, but it collapsed within weeks after Iranian attacks on shipping resumed and the US reinstated its blockade. Iran has insisted it will not give up some measure of control over the waterway and has targeted vessels using a southern route through Omani waters that avoids its preferred route through Iranian waters.

Oil prices have ticked up as the conflict widens and disruptions grow in the Middle East, though prices slipped in some trading as Saudi Arabia offered more crude via Oman, with diesel near record highs.

stories.headline: US election officials prepare for chaos before midterms; Supreme Court rejects Trump mail voting limits
body: The US Supreme Court has blocked President Donald Trump's efforts to impose new mail-in voting restrictions before the November midterm elections, a ruling that ensures the US Postal Service will continue delivering ballots as usual. The decision allows states to continue administering mail-in voting under their existing procedures. Mail-in and absentee ballots have been used in the United States for decades and now account for roughly a third of votes cast nationwide. Voting by mail has already started in states including Alabama, North Carolina and Wisconsin, with more states set to follow soon.

Trump lashed out at the court after the verdict, saying, "These are not the people I interviewed to serve on the United States Supreme Court." He called the justices "merely a shell of their original selves, a court that is costing the United States Trillions of Dollars with shockingly bad rulings." The ruling comes after Trump signed an executive order in March 2026 directing the US Postal Service to take control of mail-in voting by designing new envelopes with special barcodes that would allow the federal government to ensure ballots are only from eligible voters. That order would have forced all states to adopt a uniform envelope style in a short time, required states to provide the Postal Service with a list of eligible voters before elections, and empowered the postal agency to deny mailed ballots that did not comply with new standards or were not associated with registered voters.

Despite the ruling, political analysts and some officials fear that Trump may not let the electoral process proceed as planned and might use other federal powers to tilt the election in his favour. A Reuters investigation based on interviews with dozens of state and local election officials found that they are adopting new strategies to prepare for political interference, misinformation, cyberattacks and intimidation tactics. More than a dozen local and state election officials said they are hiring outside lawyers or seeking legal training to prepare for potential demands by the administration for access to sensitive voting records or election equipment. Nearly twice that many said they are expanding public outreach and social media campaigns to counter misinformation, including false claims by Trump and Republican allies that voting machines are unreliable and mail-in voting is inherently corrupt.

Campaigners have fiercely resisted Trump's executive actions attempting to dictate federal voting procedures. Groups including the American Civil Liberties Union (ACLU) and the Brennan Center for Justice have sued the administration, arguing that the Constitution gives authority over federal elections primarily to states and Congress, rather than the president. A bipartisan group of 261 current and former members of Congress filed a brief with the Supreme Court challenging the executive order and the subsequent Postal Service rule, arguing the measures violated the separation of powers. "The Constitution is clear that the states and Congress make the rules for federal elections, not the President," said Democratic Representative Jamie Raskin, who described the attempt to use the US Postal Service to regulate mailed ballots as "a naked power grab" and an effort "to inject confusion and chaos into our elections in a last-ditch effort to keep his party in power." Senator Alex Padilla, the top Democrat on the Senate Rules Committee, said restricting voting by mail could particularly affect military personnel, people living in rural areas, and Americans living abroad.

The White House rejected accusations that it is seeking to interfere in the midterms, saying its measures are aimed at preventing illegal voting and ensuring confidence in the electoral system. Trump has long cast doubt on the security of mail-in voting, citing debunked claims of widespread election fraud. He falsely blamed his 2020 presidential election loss on mail-in voting fraud, calling the system "the greatest scam in the history of politics." He has also pushed for the Safeguard American Voter Eligibility Act (SAVE Act), which would require citizens to provide "documentary proof" of citizenship when registering to vote; the legislation is stalled in the Senate over concerns that millions of voters would be disenfranchised. Studies show that voter fraud is extremely rare: the Heritage Foundation, the conservative-leaning think tank behind Project 2025, documented 100 cases of noncitizens voting from 1982 to 2025, about 0.000008 percent of more than 1.3 billion votes cast in presidential elections during that time.

Trump has been explicit about his desire to assert more federal control over elections, saying in early February that "Republicans ought to nationalise the voting." The attorney general has demanded that 47 states and Washington, DC, hand over their complete voter registration lists, according to a tally from the Brennan Center for Justice. Eleven states have complied or agreed to comply, while the Trump administration has launched lawsuits against the 20 others that refused. The Supreme Court ruling ensures that eligible voters who vote by mail may have their ballots on the way to them now; election officials suggest sending completed ballots back as soon as possible and checking state deadlines for requesting one.

stories.headline: Silver Defends Clippers Penalties in Kawhi Case; Leonard Not Suspended
body: NBA Commissioner Adam Silver defended the league's punishment of the Los Angeles Clippers in the Kawhi Leonard salary cap scandal, calling the sanctions 'appropriate consequences' for the organization. The NBA imposed a record $30 million fine on the Clippers, stripped them of five first-round draft picks, and suspended owner Steve Ballmer for one year after an investigation uncovered a scheme in which the team used sponsorship deals to funnel millions in under-the-table payments to Leonard and his uncle, Dennis Robertson.

Leonard, who was traded back to the Toronto Raptors, received a $700,000 restitution order but was not suspended by the NBA, and his contract was not voided. Robertson was banned from all future business dealings with NBA teams for five years. The scandal has also drawn federal and Securities and Exchange Commission probes into the illicit side deals.

ESPN's Shams Charania explained why the league did not take harsher action against Leonard, citing collective bargaining agreement restrictions and the role of the National Basketball Players Association. 'It's hard for the league because of how the collective bargaining agreement is, and there is a players union,' Charania said. He added that voiding Leonard's contract or administering a suspension would have required 'a stone cold case' to withstand litigation and arbitration from the players' union.

The investigation, which spanned a year, found that the Clippers acted like 'a power agent, brokering deals' for Robertson on Leonard's behalf, according to Charania. The team funneled endorsement income to Leonard during the 2020 and 2021 seasons through sponsors such as Aspiration and Daktronics, with Leonard not required to fulfill any real obligations in return. Reporting also detailed Robertson's alleged requests to teams over the years, including partial ownership stakes, a private plane, and a guaranteed house, all outside the bounds of the collective bargaining agreement.

The punishment drew sharp criticism from ESPN commentator Stephen A. Smith, who called Leonard 'a gangster' for avoiding significant penalty. 'He broke the rules, got caught, pointed the finger at somebody else, threw the organization under the bus, got his money and left the country,' Smith said on 'First Take.' Leonard, who waived a $7.45 million trade kicker to facilitate his return to Toronto, 'let management take the bullet while he skated away untouched,' Smith added.

With the investigation closed and Leonard's trade finalized, the league's sanctions are seen as a message to the NBA's owner class about compliance with salary cap rules. The Clippers' penalties represent the most severe in league history, while Leonard's light punishment underscores the legal constraints the NBA faced in disciplining a player under the collective bargaining agreement and union protections.

stories.headline: Manchester United scramble to keep JJ Gabriel after planned record debut collapses
body: Manchester United are scrambling to keep 15-year-old forward JJ Gabriel after the teenager decided he wants to leave the club, reversing plans that would have seen him become the club's youngest ever player. The decision comes a week after Gabriel scored a hat-trick on his Uefa Youth League debut, which had been seen as a prelude to a senior debut against Brighton in the Carabao Cup third round on Wednesday. Chief executive Omar Berrada and director of football Jason Wilcox are now involved in talks aimed at persuading Gabriel to stay, though sources describe the effort as a 'forlorn task'.

Gabriel was named Under-18 Premier League player of the year last season despite being only 14 when the campaign began, scoring 23 goals in the league and three in the FA Youth Cup. He was also United's Under-18 Player of the Year. One United source recently described him as 'the best 15-year-old in Europe'. His talent has attracted attention from Real Madrid, Barcelona and Paris St-Germain, who all focus on elite youth players. Gabriel's potential is not confined to England; he holds a European Union passport through his mother's Greek-Cypriot heritage and his father's two caps for the Republic of Ireland.

The deterioration in relations stems from a belief that promises made to Gabriel about his career path have not been kept. After committing his short-term future to United last summer, he did begin training with the senior squad under Ruben Amorim and then Michael Carrick. However, a senior debut last season was ruled out by then-interim manager Darren Fletcher, who felt it was too early. During pre-season, Gabriel played only eight minutes in a friendly against Atletico Madrid and was an unused substitute in a match against Rosenborg. It was noted that 18-year-old Tynan Thompson, who joined from Tottenham three weeks earlier, made a 45-minute senior debut against Leeds United in a match Gabriel also travelled to but did not feature in.

Gabriel had been expected to make his senior debut this autumn, likely in the EFL Cup. But when United faced Sabah FK in the Uefa Youth League, Gabriel could not be used as a substitute because of Uefa registration rules: as a 15-year-old, he needed to be on the club's A list of players for the senior squad, yet United did not name him on that list. The club's coaches have suggested Gabriel is not yet at the required physical level, but sources close to the player reject that, pointing to Arsenal giving 15-year-old Max Dowman a chance and Bayern Munich giving 17-year-old Lennart Karl a debut.

Gabriel's registration with United runs until the end of the season, which may buy time regarding moves to Premier League rivals. But European clubs could exploit his EU passport. Legal precedents exist: in 2019, 16-year-old Louie Barry left West Brom for Barcelona with West Brom receiving no compensation after failing to formally offer him a scholarship. A worst-case scenario for United would be Gabriel walking away when he turns 16 on 6 October, potentially leaving the club with no compensation for a player whose market value, even at this age, is measured in millions.

The situation echoes other youth transfers. Jadon Sancho was 17 when he stopped training at Manchester City to force a £10m move to Borussia Dortmund. Morgan Rogers left West Brom for Manchester City on his 17th birthday. United Under-21s coach Adam Lawrence, after Gabriel's Youth League hat-trick, said: 'The first thing in my job is not to ruin him... you obviously don't want to stifle their freedom and their creativity.' For now, Berrada and Wilcox are trying to prevent a second thing: losing him entirely.

stories.headline: Charlotte to Host WTA Finals From 2027; Tour Takes Over Operations
body: The WTA Finals, the season-ending championship for women's tennis, will be held in Charlotte, North Carolina, for a minimum of three years beginning in 2027, the WTA and the Charlotte Sports Foundation jointly announced Wednesday. The event will take place at the Spectrum Center, home of the NBA's Charlotte Hornets. Under the agreement, the WTA will also relocate its global headquarters from St. Petersburg, Florida, to Charlotte and has pledged to create a path toward bringing a WTA 500 tournament to the city after 2029.

WTA chair Valerie Camillo said the tour is taking operational control of the Finals for the first time, moving away from the previous model of receiving licensing fees from host cities. "The WTA has always owned the WTA Finals, but now going forward, we're going to operate it too," Camillo said. "We're taking control of the creation of the revenues and the controlling of the expenses and the delivery of the entire thing. And that allows us to control our own destiny." Camillo's ambition, she stated, is for the Finals to become "the Super Bowl for women's sports," adding that audiences and investment in women's athletics are growing.

The Finals, which feature the year's top eight singles players and doubles teams, have had six different hosts in seven years after a planned 10-year stay in Shenzhen, China, ended after a single edition. Subsequent stops included Guadalajara, Fort Worth, Cancun, and Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, where crowds were frequently sparse. This year's tournament will be held in Indian Wells, California, after the WTA opted out of the final year of a three-year hosting deal with Saudi Arabia. Camillo cited the unexpected cost of that relocation and ongoing belt-tightening as part of a transition year for the tour in 2026.

The move to the Spectrum Center — an NBA arena that will be in regular-season use during the Finals — will compress the tournament schedule from eight days to five. Camillo said the WTA is exploring alternate formats with players; if the round-robin component remains, finalists would need to play every day. Prize money for the Charlotte edition has not been announced. The prize pool for this year's Finals in Indian Wells is $10 million, $5.5 million less than the sum put up by Saudi Arabia last year. In 2025, winner Elena Rybakina earned a women's-sports-record payout of approximately $5.3 million in Riyadh.

The WTA described the Charlotte arrangement as a minimum three-year deal. Financial backing comes from regional economic enterprises, local government funding, and investment from Charlotte's corporate community, according to the Charlotte Sports Foundation. Spectrum Center has previously hosted high-profile tennis exhibitions.

Camillo indicated the tour will continue seeking control over its own media rights and calendar. Asked about a potential merger with the men's ATP Finals, she said there had not been an in-depth conversation on that topic, adding: "I think that when we create our ambition, people are going to want to merge with us on this event and many more." This year's WTA Finals will run Nov. 7-14 in Indian Wells.

stories.headline: 2030 Winter Olympics venues confirmed; speed skating in Netherlands
body: The International Olympic Committee (IOC) on Wednesday confirmed the 11 competition venues for the 2030 Winter Games, with events split across southern France and, for the first time in Olympic history, an independent nation outside the host region: the Netherlands will host the long track speed skating events.

Lyon will serve as the ice sports hub, hosting curling, figure skating, and short track speed skating at three sites including Parc Olympique Lyonnais, home of Ligue 1 side Lyon. Alpine skiing speed events — downhill, super-G, and team events — will be held in Courchevel, while Val d'Isere stages the slalom events. The long track speed skating competitions will take place at the Thialf arena in Heerenveen, Netherlands, a pre-existing facility chosen to avoid building new venues without a clear legacy in the host region.

The announcement caps a turbulent period for the 2030 Games organisers. In May, the ice sports hub was moved from Nice to Lyon after Nice's mayor, Eric Ciotti, refused to allow the city's football stadium to be converted into a temporary ice rink. Last month, organising committee president Edgar Grospiron resigned after just 18 months in the role, amid budget cuts for the Games.

The 2030 Winter Olympics will feature 16 sporting disciplines, including two new additions: freeride skiing and snowboarding, and synchro9 — synchronised figure skating. However, the Games will be the first not to include nordic combined, which has been removed from the programme.

Holding the speed skating in the Netherlands was a condition agreed with the IOC when the French Alps were awarded the Games, as organisers sought to reduce costs by using an existing arena rather than constructing a new one. This marks the first time an Olympic event — summer or winter — will be held in a different independent nation from the host city or region.

stories.headline: Senate panel weighs Trump's third surgeon general pick and two other HHS nominees
body: The Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions meets Wednesday to consider three of President Donald Trump's nominees for top jobs at the Department of Health and Human Services: Dr. Nicole Saphier for surgeon general, Chris Klomp for deputy secretary, and Dr. Timothy Westlake for assistant secretary for Mental Health and Substance Use. The hearing comes after the committee never voted on Trump's previous surgeon general nominee, Dr. Casey Means, whose support collapsed following a contentious February hearing and a last-minute cancellation of her first hearing because she went into labor. Means was the second nominee; Trump's first choice, Fox News medical contributor Dr. Janette Nesheiwat, was dropped after questions about her academic credentials. The United States has not had a surgeon general since President Biden left office in January 2025.

Saphier, a radiologist and director of breast imaging at Memorial Sloan Kettering Monmouth in New Jersey, is also a former Fox News Channel contributor and a health and wellness influencer with nearly 360,000 followers on X and 147,000 on Instagram, where she identifies herself as a "full time wife, mom and doctor." She is the creator of Drop Rx, a brand of liquid herbal supplements; the site notes its statements have not been evaluated by the Food and Drug Administration and that products are not intended to diagnose, treat, cure, or prevent disease, with many products currently unavailable online and some selling for $24.99 for 2 fluid ounces. Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. praised her nomination in April, calling her "a long-time warrior for the MAHA movement"—she wrote a book titled "Make America Healthy Again" in 2020, years before Kennedy adopted the slogan. Unlike Means, Saphier's nomination has not met a wall of opposition, and former Surgeon General Jerome Adams, who served in Trump's first term, told NPR in May he expects her to be confirmed.

A key issue at the hearing will likely be Saphier's views on vaccines. She has criticized COVID-19 vaccine booster requirements and questioned whether every child needs the hepatitis B vaccine at birth—comments that may draw attention from Republican Sen. Bill Cassidy, a liver doctor and committee chair who has spoken emotionally about treating patients who died of hepatitis B. However, she has defended vaccines in the context of the debunked link with autism; in an op-ed last spring, she criticized Kennedy's decision to hire anti-vaccine activist David Geier to investigate rising autism diagnoses, writing, "If we want lasting change in how we diagnose, treat and perhaps prevent autism, it must be built on a foundation of rigorous science, not controversy and conspiracy theories." She also told The Associated Press last fall that Trump's suggestion that pregnant women avoid Tylenol because of autism risk was oversimplistic and "patronizing."

Experts say bringing an influencer into the surgeon general role—often called the nation's doctor—presents both opportunities and challenges. A Pew Research Center report published earlier this year found 4 in 10 U.S. adults overall, and half of those under 50, get health and wellness information from social media influencers and podcasts, but less than half of influencer profiles describe themselves as health professionals; about 1 in 8 cite personal experience, and nearly 1 in 6 mention no background or expertise. Only about 10% of adults say they trust all or most influencer information, while a quarter trust not much or none. Adams said the distinction matters: "An influencer builds a brand and an audience. The surgeon general speaks for the nation (and not just 'followers'), leads the Public Health Service Commissioned Corps, and has a duty to follow evidence even when it is politically inconvenient." stories.headline: OpenAI confirms joint AI safety talks with Anthropic and Google DeepMind
stories.byline: Tech / AI desk · anchored on Reuters
body: OpenAI has confirmed that it has been in talks with rivals Anthropic and Google DeepMind for several weeks regarding AI safety, according to a report by Bloomberg. The company's global policy chief, Chris Lehane, disclosed the discussions during a Tuesday briefing in Washington, D.C., saying, “It’s better to try to work together to prioritize safety.” The confirmation follows earlier reporting from The Information and an interview in which OpenAI CEO Sam Altman hinted at private discussions with other AI leaders.

The collaborative talks have roots in a July proposal from Google DeepMind chair Demis Hassabis, who called for a U.S.-led “Standards Body” — structured as a public-private partnership or a self-regulatory organization with federal oversight, similar to the Financial Industry Regulatory Authority — that could screen advanced AI models and coordinate industrywide slowdowns if dangers emerged. An OpenAI spokesperson confirmed to CNBC that the companies have been discussing the proposal since its release. Lehane argued that no antitrust waiver is necessary for the coordination, comparing it to safety cooperation in the commercial airline industry.

The announcement follows a 3,800-word essay published Saturday by Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, who urged AI companies to slow the pace of frontier model development so researchers can better understand potential catastrophic risks. Amodei’s call received backing from OpenAI’s Sam Altman, Google DeepMind’s Demis Hassabis, and xAI founder Elon Musk. Altman posted on X that a slowdown has been a “primary topic” of discussion at OpenAI in recent weeks and that the company will have more to share “soon.” Hassabis wrote that Amodei’s essay “points towards the right path forward.”

The prospect of direct competitors coordinating on safety has drawn scrutiny from antitrust regulators. FTC Chair Andrew Ferguson, speaking Tuesday, said he would be “deeply suspicious” of requests for antitrust exemptions, viewing the coordination as an attempt to create barriers to entry that insulate incumbent firms from challengers. “That sure sounds like moat digging,” Ferguson said, according to Bloomberg.

Lehane, who is in Washington working with lawmakers, said OpenAI is prepared to back bipartisan legislation targeting catastrophic AI risks. The company supports a federal governance framework proposed by Representative Jay Obernolte (R-CA) and Representative Lori Trahan (D-MA), as well as a Senate effort led by Majority Leader John Thune (R-SD), along with Senators Ted Cruz (R-TX) and Amy Klobuchar (D-MN). OpenAI also supports a provision in the FRONTIER Act that would require top frontier labs to allow independent verification organizations into their companies to ensure safe model development, according to TechCrunch. However, any AI bill becoming law before the end of 2026 is considered a long shot, as the House departs Washington on Thursday and has no scheduled sessions before the November election.

stories.headline: SpaceX declares Starship ready for orbital attempt, sets launch date of September 22
body: SpaceX announced Tuesday that it intends to launch the 14th test flight of its Starship rocket as soon as September 22, pending regulatory approval. The mission will be the first time the company attempts to put the Starship upper stage into orbit around Earth. Liftoff from SpaceX’s facility in Brownsville, Texas, is targeted for 7:15 a.m. CT (12:15 UTC) within a 75-minute launch window.

For this flight, Starship will carry 26 of SpaceX’s third-generation V3 Starlink satellites to an orbit 275 kilometers above Earth. The upper stage is expected to complete six orbits over roughly 10 hours before ending its mission. If successful, the deployment would mark the first Starship launch to generate revenue for SpaceX’s launch division, even if the customer is another part of the company.

SpaceX detailed design changes to the Super Heavy booster following issues on the previous flight, which occurred on July 24. During that test, the booster’s three center engines showed signs of ice clogging during the return through the atmosphere, triggering an early end to the maneuver. The booster attempted a landing burn with 8 of 13 planned engines reigniting before making a hard splashdown in the Gulf of Mexico. SpaceX said the Super Heavy on the upcoming flight has hardware modifications to improve engine filtering and software changes to enhance relight reliability.

The company also said it made additional changes to the Starship heat shield based on what it learned from studying the recovered upper stage from the July test. That flight was the first to successfully deploy V3 Starlink satellites, though those burned up in the atmosphere after roughly 20 minutes. The upper stage had a smooth simulated landing in the Indian Ocean and did not explode when it tipped over, allowing SpaceX to recover and tow it back to Texas for analysis.

SpaceX will not attempt to catch either the Super Heavy booster or the Starship upper stage with the launch tower on this flight, following founder and CEO Elon Musk’s statement that an explosion would be too big a setback for the company. Reaching orbit would represent a major milestone in Starship’s development, which began with its first test flight on April 20, 2023. SpaceX aims to eventually retire its Falcon 9 and Falcon Heavy rockets in favor of Starship once the vehicle is flying reliably multiple times per week, a cadence the company promised during its initial public offering process in June.
